cards.title: Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)
cards.question: Explain Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)
cards.answer_30s: The GIL is a mutex in CPython that allows only one native thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, simplifying C-extension memory management. It limits CPU-bound multi-threading to a single core, while I/O-bound threads release the GIL during blocking OS calls.

code.body:
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, ThreadPoolExecutor

# CPU-bound: bypasses GIL with separate processes
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(heavy_compute, items))

# I/O-bound: threads release GIL while waiting on network
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=20) as pool:
    responses = list(pool.map(fetch_url, urls))

cards.typical_use: Choosing between multiprocessing, threading, and asyncio in backend services.
pitfalls: Mention that Python 3.13 introduced experimental free-threaded builds (--disable-gil), and libraries like NumPy release the GIL inside C routines.

cards.title: Asyncio Event Loop & Coroutines
cards.question: Explain Asyncio Event Loop & Coroutines
cards.answer_30s: Asyncio enables cooperative single-threaded concurrency using an event loop that schedules coroutines when they yield control at await points. It excels at high-concurrency I/O-bound workloads like HTTP clients, WebSockets, and async DB drivers.

code.body:
import asyncio

async def fetch_all(urls):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)
    async def bounded_fetch(u):
        async with sem:
            return await fetch_one(u)
    tasks = [bounded_fetch(u) for u in urls]
    return await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)

cards.typical_use: Handling thousands of concurrent API or database calls without thread-pool overhead.
pitfalls: Never call blocking synchronous functions (like time.sleep or requests.get) inside an async def coroutine; use asyncio.to_thread() to offload them.

cards.title: Generators, Iterators & Lazy Evaluation
cards.question: Explain Generators, Iterators & Lazy Evaluation
cards.answer_30s: Iterators implement __iter__ and __next__ to yield items on demand. Generators use the yield keyword to pause execution and preserve local stack state, processing massive datasets in O(1) memory instead of materializing full lists.
cards.typical_use: Streaming multi-gigabyte files, ETL pipelines, and paginated API responses.
pitfalls: Distinguish generator expressions (x for x in seq) from list comprehensions [x for x in seq] when memory efficiency matters.

cards.title: Decorators, Closures & functools.wraps
cards.question: Explain Decorators, Closures & functools.wraps
cards.answer_30s: A closure captures variables from its enclosing lexical scope even after the outer function returns. Decorators wrap functions or classes to add cross-cutting behavior like logging, caching, or auth checks; functools.wraps preserves the original __name__ and __doc__.
cards.typical_use: Implementing retry logic, rate limiting, auth guards, and telemetry instrumentation.
pitfalls: Forgetting @wraps breaks FastAPI/pytest introspection and hides the wrapped function's signature.

cards.title: Data Structure Complexities
cards.question: Explain Data Structure Complexities
cards.answer_30s: Lists are dynamic arrays with O(1) random access and amortized append, but O(n) insert/pop at index 0. Dicts and sets use open-addressed hash tables with O(1) average lookup. collections.deque provides O(1) append and popleft at both ends.

code.body:
from collections import deque, Counter

q = deque(maxlen=100)
q.append(1)
q.popleft()  # O(1) vs list.pop(0) O(n)
counts = Counter(['a', 'b', 'a'])

cards.typical_use: Optimizing hot loops, sliding windows, and membership checks.
pitfalls: In Python 3.7+, dict preserves insertion order by language specification. Membership checks (x in set_or_dict) are O(1) vs O(n) for lists.

cards.title: Memory Management & Garbage Collection
cards.question: Explain Memory Management & Garbage Collection
cards.answer_30s: CPython uses immediate reference counting for deterministic deallocation when an object's refcount hits zero, paired with a generational cyclic garbage collector (generations 0, 1, 2) to detect and free reference cycles.
cards.typical_use: Reducing memory footprint by 40-60% in data-intensive services with millions of objects.
pitfalls: Explain __slots__ trade-offs: prevents dynamic attribute assignment and weakens multiple inheritance, but drastically cuts memory per instance.

cards.title: Context Managers & Resource Lifecycle
cards.question: Explain Context Managers & Resource Lifecycle
cards.answer_30s: Context managers implement __enter__ and __exit__ (or use @contextmanager) to guarantee setup and deterministic cleanup even when exceptions occur. They prevent leaked file descriptors, locks, and database connections.
cards.typical_use: Managing DB transactions, distributed locks, temporary files, and HTTP sessions.
pitfalls: Mention async context managers (__aenter__ / __aexit__) used with async with for async DB pools and httpx clients.

cards.title: Descriptors, Properties & Metaclasses
cards.question: Explain Descriptors, Properties & Metaclasses
cards.answer_30s: Descriptors implement __get__, __set__, or __delete__ to customize attribute access (powering @property, classmethod, and ORM fields). Metaclasses (type subclasses) control class creation itself, enabling registration or validation at import time.
cards.typical_use: Understanding how Django ORM models, SQLAlchemy columns, and Pydantic validators work internally.
pitfalls: Quote Tim Peters: if you wonder whether you need a metaclass, you don't—prefer __init_subclass__ or class decorators for simpler hooks.

cards.title: Testing, Fixtures & Monkeypatching with Pytest
cards.question: Explain Testing, Fixtures & Monkeypatching with Pytest
cards.answer_30s: Pytest uses dependency-injected fixtures with scoped lifecycles (function, module, session), parametrized test matrices, and monkeypatch/unittest.mock to isolate external I/O and verify edge cases cleanly.
cards.typical_use: Maintaining fast, deterministic CI pipelines without hitting live external APIs.
pitfalls: Always mock at the boundary where the dependency is imported, not where it is defined.

cards.title: Secure Serialization, Subprocess & Input Handling
cards.question: Explain Secure Serialization, Subprocess & Input Handling
cards.answer_30s: Never unpickle untrusted data because pickle can execute arbitrary code via __reduce__. Use json or Pydantic schemas, avoid shell=True in subprocess calls, and load secrets from environment managers.

code.body:
import subprocess, json

# Safe: argument list without shell interpolation
subprocess.run(['ls', '-la', safe_dir], check=True, shell=False)
data = json.loads(raw_body)

cards.typical_use: Hardening Python microservices against RCE and command injection.
pitfalls: Highlight yaml.safe_load() over yaml.load(), and secrets.compare_digest() for constant-time token comparison.

cards.title: Q: Why does a mutable default argument cause bugs in Python?
cards.question: Q: Why does a mutable default argument cause bugs in Python?
cards.answer_30s: A: Default argument values are evaluated once at function definition time (def), not on each call. Using a mutable object like [] or {} causes every call without that argument to mutate the same shared object. Fix it by defaulting to None and initializing inside the function body.
cards.typical_use: Preventing subtle cross-request state leakage in shared helpers.
pitfalls: Note that dataclass fields have the same trap—use field(default_factory=list) there.

cards.title: Q: What is the difference between == and is, and shallow vs deep copy?
cards.question: Q: What is the difference between == and is, and shallow vs deep copy?
cards.answer_30s: A: == checks value equality (__eq__), while is checks object identity (same memory address via id()). Shallow copy (copy.copy / list.copy) creates a new outer container referencing the same nested objects; copy.deepcopy recursively copies all nested objects.

code.body:
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = copy.copy(a)
shallow[0].append(99)  # Mutates a[0] too!
deep = copy.deepcopy(a)

cards.typical_use: Avoiding accidental mutation of shared nested config dictionaries.
pitfalls: Always use 'is None' (not '== None') because custom __eq__ implementations can override ==.

cards.title: Q: How do *args, **kwargs, and late-binding closures work?
cards.question: Q: How do *args, **kwargs, and late-binding closures work?
cards.answer_30s: A: *args packs positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs packs keyword arguments into a dict. Late-binding closures look up loop variables when the inner function is called, not when it is created; bind the loop variable via a default argument (lambda x=i: x) to capture the current value.

code.body:
# Fixing late-binding closure in a loop
funcs = [lambda i=i: i * 2 for i in range(3)]
assert [f() for f in funcs] == [0, 2, 4]

cards.typical_use: Debugging callback factories and dynamic event handlers.
pitfalls: This late-binding closure trap is one of the most common senior Python live-coding questions.

cards.title: Q: How does Python's MRO (Method Resolution Order) work with multiple inheritance?
cards.question: Q: How does Python's MRO (Method Resolution Order) work with multiple inheritance?
cards.answer_30s: A: Python uses C3 Linearization to compute a deterministic, monotonic MRO (__mro__) that preserves local precedence and ensures parent classes are searched after their children. super() delegates to the next class in the MRO, enabling cooperative multiple inheritance.

code.body:
class A: pass
class B(A): pass
class C(A): pass
class D(B, C): pass
print([cls.__name__ for cls in D.__mro__])  # D, B, C, A, object

cards.typical_use: Designing clean mixin hierarchies in Django/FastAPI class utilities.
pitfalls: Explain the diamond problem and why super() does not just mean 'my direct parent'—it means 'next in MRO'.

cards.title: Q: How do you diagnose and fix a memory leak in a long-running Python service?
cards.question: Q: How do you diagnose and fix a memory leak in a long-running Python service?
cards.answer_30s: A: Use tracemalloc to snapshot and diff allocations over time, objgraph or gc.get_objects() to find growing reference types, and check common culprits: unbounded in-memory caches (missing maxsize on lru_cache), global lists, circular references with __del__, or unclosed file/DB handles.

code.body:
import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
snap1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
# ... run workload ...
snap2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for stat in snap2.compare_to(snap1, 'lineno')[:5]:
    print(stat)

cards.typical_use: Resolving OOMKills in production worker pods and API servers.
pitfalls: Always mention @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1024) or cachetools.TTLCache instead of unbounded dicts.

cards.title: Q: When should you choose Python over Go or Rust, and how do you scale Python?
cards.question: Q: When should you choose Python over Go or Rust, and how do you scale Python?
cards.answer_30s: A: Choose Python for rapid iteration, rich data/ML ecosystems, and I/O-bound APIs where developer velocity dominates. Scale it horizontally behind load balancers using multiple Uvicorn/Gunicorn workers (one per core), async I/O, Redis caching, Celery/worker queues for background tasks, and C/Rust extensions (Polars, Pydantic v2, NumPy) for hot paths.
cards.typical_use: System design and architectural trade-off discussions.
pitfalls: Highlight that Pydantic v2 moved core validation to Rust (pydantic-core), giving 5-50x speedups while keeping Python ergonomics.
